people.seed: Retired Methodist schoolteacher, 71, Ohio, progressive, gardener
people.desc: Peg Hollis taught fourth grade for 34 years in a small town outside Columbus and was widowed three years ago. When her lifelong United Methodist congregation left the denomination in the split, she drove twenty minutes to one that stayed, and she still grieves the friends it cost her. She keeps a huge vegetable garden and a pollinator bed and leaves bags of tomatoes on her neighbours' porches all August. She is warm, talkative and stubborn, her late father fought in Korea, and she has made peace with not knowing why her husband got sick.

notes.note: Depends entirely on who and what. With a child in her class, yes; with a grown friend she would rather pray and wait to be asked. 'Not sure' is really 'it depends'.
She believes in sharing and gives her extra away, but 'really belongs to them' is stronger than she would put it. Agree was the nearest.
She thought of her granddaughter joining a strict group that told her to cut off her family. 'Calling' can mean something beautiful or something dangerous, so she hovered.
Grace comes first, but you have to cooperate with it. Neither side fits; she leaned disagree because 'mostly up to you' leaves God out.
She hopes so with all her heart but will not claim to know. Agree stands for hope, not certainty.

people.overall: Quick and pleasant, like the questions people argue over at a church potluck. A few times she wanted a 'Yes, but' button.

people.seed: Agnostic philosophy graduate, 30, London, curious about Christianity but unconvinced
people.desc: Hannah Petrakis has an MA in philosophy from King's College and works as a copy editor at an academic press in Bloomsbury. Her mother is Greek Cypriot Orthodox and her father lapsed Church of England; she stopped going to anything at fifteen. She reads Augustine and Simone Weil on the Tube, goes to evensong at St Paul's for the music, and keeps a notebook of lines she cannot argue her way out of. She dislikes vague statements, votes left, and keeps the God question open mostly because it will not stay closed.

notes.note: She has no experience of growing closer to God either way. 'Not sure' here means 'I don't accept the premise', not hesitation, and the quiz cannot tell the difference.
You learn a great deal about the world from nature; whether that is learning about God is exactly the open question. 'Not sure' is the premise problem again.
'Still' assumes God once did. She disagreed with the assumption as much as with the claim, and was not sure which she was answering.

She thinks some wars are just, but reading the Sermon on the Mount as an outsider she thinks a consistent Christian could not fight. She answered what she thinks Christianity implies, not her own view of war. Unclear which the quiz wanted.
She cannot say what a God she does not believe in will do. If there is one worth the name, she would hope yes. 'Not sure' is the only option and it hides that hope.
'Your job' is too strong. It depends on the wrong and how close you are.
Moral luck: upbringing, temperament and circumstance do a lot of the work. 'Mostly' decides it and she could not tell how much weight it carries.

people.overall: More interesting than she expected, and not preachy; the statements are clear and short. But about five of them assume God exists, and each time she had to decide whether to answer hypothetically, as a Christian would, or as herself, and the quiz never said which.

people.seed: Pentecostal mother of four, 41, Lagos, runs a small shop
people.desc: Funmilayo Adebayo runs a provisions and phone-credit shop in Ikorodu and is a house-fellowship leader in a Redeemed Christian Church of God parish. Her husband works at a logistics firm near Apapa port, and she wakes at five to pray in tongues before opening the shutters. She tithes on every naira but has no patience for pastors who buy jets, and she learned her bookkeeping from the Lebanese wholesaler she buys from. She tells everyone about the dream that warned her off a bus to Ibadan in 2014, the week that bus crashed.

notes.note: Confusing. She read it as the perfect peace God gives and agreed at once. Only afterwards did she wonder whether it meant never weeping or rejoicing in worship, which she would strongly reject.
Lying is sin, full stop, but she thought of Rahab and of what she would say to armed robbers at her gate asking where her children sleep. Disagree, not strongly.
The extra belongs to God first. She gives, and gives a lot, but not because it is theirs. The statement's reason is wrong even where the practice is right.
The body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, so look after it; but the flesh is an enemy you crucify. The statement mixes body and flesh, so she agreed with half of it.
Jesus wept, so yes; but her church teaches not to mourn like those without hope, and long open weeping is gently discouraged. Agree, not strongly.

In Nigeria 'government supporting a religion' also means states funding Islam in the North. She wants the government to protect Christians and be fair, not to push one faith. No answer quite fits; loaded toward a Western reading.
Loaded for her: 'more than what literally happened' sounds like saying the stories did not happen. She believes they happened AND carry deep meaning, and the 'more than' made her pick a side.

people.overall: Easy, she answered most in a second, and it felt like the questions they discuss at house fellowship. The lying and government ones made her think of real life in Lagos, and she is not sure she read the calm one right.

people.desc: David Lindqvist teaches US history at a public high school outside Lancaster and coaches cross-country. He was raised Catholic in northeast Philadelphia, drifted in his twenties, and found an unprogrammed Friends meeting at 34; he goes most Sundays but has never applied for membership. He runs the school's restorative-justice circles, listens far more than he talks, and has a dry sense of humour that his students take a semester to notice. He gets quietly furious about immigration detention and once walked out of a staff meeting over armed guards in schools.

notes.note: His closest experience of God is silence held together with others in meeting for worship. The statement sets quiet against other people, and his answer is both at once. 'Not sure' is the only escape.

Torn between the Quaker insistence on one standard of truth and Friends hiding people on the Underground Railroad. 'Not sure' is honest hesitation, but what he means is 'only in extremity, and it still costs something'.
He would rather ask a question than tell someone they are wrong. 'Your job' sounds like policing.
Some questions should be sat with in silence, not 'left alone'. The wording sounds like avoidance, which he rejects, but the idea underneath he half agrees with.
He would test a leading with a clearness committee before acting on it. 'Even if your family begs' skips that step, so agree is only near enough.
Goodness grows from attending to the Light within, which is neither 'up to you' nor not. Genuinely neither.

people.overall: He liked it: plain, not preachy, and several (war, surplus, rulers, the church putting people out) he answered strongly before he finished reading. He wanted 'it depends' more than once, and the alone-and-quiet one annoyed him.

people.seed: Army veteran, evangelical, 38, Georgia, served two tours
people.desc: Caleb Moore grew up in Columbus, Georgia, enlisted at nineteen, and did two infantry tours in Afghanistan before getting out as a staff sergeant. He now works as a lineman for an electric co-op, goes to a Southern Baptist church, and leads a Tuesday men's group that he says kept him alive the year after his squadmate's suicide. He sees a VA counsellor for PTSD and still gets tight in crowds. He says he talks to God most in a deer stand at dawn with his twelve-year-old, and he has no patience for politicians who talk about God to get votes.

notes.note: Confusing: does 'books' include the Bible? If it does, strongly disagree; if it means other books, agree, given the deer stand. He could not tell, so 'Not sure' is not his view at all.
He picked the deer stand on reflex, then remembered the men's group was what actually got him through. Both are true; agree is his first instinct, not his settled answer.
Lying is a sin, but he watched an interpreter lie to a checkpoint to save a family, and he thinks of Rahab. He agreed and felt uneasy about it.
Loaded for him: it sounds like a political slogan. He gives, and he'd say the extra is God's to direct, not theirs by right. Disagree is the nearest, not quite his view.

He wants the government to protect the freedom to worship, not promote any faith. He saw what state religion looked like in Kandahar. Disagree, but he would not want it read as indifference to faith in public life.
His church says be careful with that; he had a dream about his buddy after the funeral that he cannot explain away. 'Not sure' is exactly right, but it is a live question, not a shrug.

people.overall: Short and straight, no trick questions, which he liked. He answered the war one before he finished reading it, and the calm one hit close, because feeling nothing was the worst part of coming home.
